'''''The Principles of Quantum Mechanics''''' is an influential [[monograph]] written by [[Paul Dirac]] and first published by [[Oxford University Press]] in 1930.<ref name=Nobel>
  {{cite web
  | title =Paul A.M. Dirac – Biography
  | quote = Dirac's publications include ... The Principles of Quantum Mechanics (1930; 3rd ed. 1947). 
  | publisher =The Nobel Prize in Physics 1933 
  | date = 
  | url =https://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/physics/laureates/1933/dirac-bio.html  
  | doi = 
  | accessdate =September 26, 2011}}</ref> In this book, Dirac presents [[quantum mechanics]] in a formal, logically consistent, and [[Axiom|axiomatic]] fashion,<ref name=Farmelo/> making the book the first of its kind.<ref name=":1" />{{Reference page|page=366}} It is based on [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrices]] and [[Operator (physics)|operators]] rather than [[wave–particle duality]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=French |first=A. P. |author-link=Anthony Philip French |title=An Introduction to Quantum Physics |last2=Taylor |first2=Edwin |author-link2=Edwin F. Taylor |publisher=W. W. Norton & Company |year=1978 |isbn=0-393-09106-6}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=658}} Its 82 sections contain 785 equations with no diagrams.<ref name=Farmelo>
{{cite journal
  | last =Farmelo  
  | first =Graham  
  | title =Speaking Volumes: The Principles of Quantum Mechanics 
  | journal = Times Higher Education Supplement  
  | volume = 
  | issue = 
  | pages =20 
  | format = Book review
  | date =June 2, 1995 
  | url =http://www.timeshighereducation.co.uk/story.asp?sectioncode=26&storycode=162404 
  | jstor =  
  | issn = 
  | doi = 
  | mr = 
  | zbl = 
  | jfm = 
  | accessdate =2011-09-26}}</ref> Nor does it have an index, a bibliography, or a list of suggestions for further reading.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Farmelo |first=Graham |title=The Strangest Man: The Hidden Life of Paul Dirac, Mystic of the Atom |title-link=The Strangest Man |publisher=Basic Books |year=2009 |isbn=978-0-465-02210-6}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=178}} The first half of the book lays down the foundations of quantum mechanics while the second half focuses on its applications.<ref name=":3" />  Dirac did not pursue a [[History of quantum mechanics|historical approach]] to the subject. Nor did he discuss at length the [[philosophy of quantum mechanics]].<ref name=":0" />{{Reference page|page=178}}

== History ==
Paul Dirac played a key role in the development of quantum mechanics at the [[University of Cambridge]] and the [[University of Göttingen]] during the mid- to late-1920s.<ref name="Farmelo" /> In September 1925, Dirac, then a post-graduate student, received the [[Galley proof|proofs]] of a [[Umdeutung paper|seminal paper]] forwarded to him by his supervisor, [[Ralph Fowler]], from its author, Werner Heisenberg. Dirac soon recognized the fundamental importance of the non-commutativity of the quantities he encountered. He realized that there was a connection between Heisenberg's matrices and [[Poisson bracket|Poisson brackets]] from classical mechanics, which he could exploit to create his own version of quantum mechanics.<ref name=":0" />{{Reference page|pages=83-9}} 

Dirac was one of a handful of physicists at Cambridge who were at the cutting edge of the new quantum theory, and, unusually for an early-career researcher, he agreed to write a new textbook on the subject to be published as part of the ''International Series of Monographs on Physics'', edited by Fowler and [[Peter Kapitza]].<ref name=":0" />{{Reference page|page=145}} The first edition of ''The Principles of Quantum Mechanics'' appeared in 1930.<ref name="Paul Dirac">{{cite book|last=Dalitz|first=R. H.|title=The Collected Works of P. A. M. Dirac: Volume 1: 1924–1948|year=1995|publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]]|isbn=9780521362313|pages=453–454|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=GBEdMdNWFJIC&pg=453}}</ref> ''The Principles'' was similar in style to the lectures Dirac had been delivering at Cambridge while he was a doctoral candidate during the late 1920s, but not in the contents, which were restricted to what was known at the time. After the completion of the book, Dirac used it for his courses on quantum mechanics over the next four decades, including the regular one he taught at Cambridge during the 1930s in the [[Lent]] terms (Spring). ([[Alan Herries Wilson|Alan Wilson]] taught in the [[Michaelmas]] terms (Fall), where he focused on the applications of Schrödinger's equation.)<ref name=":4" /> 

Whereas [[Erwin Schrödinger]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Schrödinger |first=Erwin |date=1926 |title=Über das Verhältnis der Heisenberg-Born-Jordanschen Quantenmechanik zu der meinen |trans-title=On the Relationship between the Heisenberg-Born-Jordan Quantum Mechanics and My Own |journal=Annalen der Physik |language=German |volume=79 |issue=8 |pages=734-56}}</ref> and [[Carl Eckart]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Eckart |first=Carl |date=1926 |title=The Solution of the Problem of the Simple Oscillator by a Combination of the Schroedinger and the Lanczos Theories |url=https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.12.7.473 |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |volume=12 |issue=7 |pages=473-6 |doi=10.1073/pnas.12.7.473|url-access=subscription |pmc=1084628 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Eckart |first=Carl |date=1926 |title=Operator Calculus and the Solution of the Equations of Quantum Dynamics |url=https://journals.aps.org/pr/abstract/10.1103/PhysRev.28.711 |journal=Physical Review |volume=28 |pages=711-26 |doi=10.1103/PhysRev.28.711}}</ref> had only demonstrated the equivalence of the [[Schrödinger equation|wave]] and [[Matrix mechanics|matrix]] formulations of quantum mechanics, Dirac went much further, creating his own version that encompassed both of the above.<ref name=":2" />{{Reference page|page=154}} He called it the theory of [[Linear map|linear transformations]]. In addition, he took inspiration from paper published by [[Cornelius Lanczos]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lanczos |first=Cornelius |date=1926 |title=Über eine feldmäßige Darstellung der neuen Quantenmechanik |trans-title=On a Field-based Representation of the New Quantum Mechanics |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF01379857 |journal=Zeitschrift für Physik |language=German |volume=35 |pages=812-30 |doi=10.1007/BF01379857|url-access=subscription }}</ref> presenting quantum mechanics in terms of the theory of linear [[Integral equation|integral equations]]. In the preface, Dirac commented, "A great deal of my work was just playing with equations and see what they give."<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Jammer |first=Max |author-link=Max Jammer |title=The Conceptual Development of Quantum Mechanics |publisher=McGraw-Hill |year=1966 |isbn=978-0-88318-617-6}}</ref>{{Reference page|pages=300-1}} In his construction of transformation theory, Dirac popularized the <math>\delta</math>-function,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Dirac |first=Paul |date=1927 |title=The Physical Interpretation of the Quantum Dynamics |url=https://royalsocietypublishing.org/rspa/article/113/765/621/2065/The-physical-interpretation-of-the-quantum |journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society of London A |volume=113 |issue=765 |pages=621–641 |doi=10.1098/rspa.1927.0012|doi-access=free }}</ref> a generalized function or distribution [[Dirac delta function|now named after him]], though it had previously been used in the nineteenth century by multiple scholars,<ref name="JacksonHistory">{{Cite journal |last=Jackson |first=John D. |author-link=John David Jackson (physicist) |date=August 1, 2008 |title=Examples of the zeroth theorem of the history of science |url=https://pubs.aip.org/aapt/ajp/article-abstract/76/8/704/1057888/Examples-of-the-zeroth-theorem-of-the-history-of?redirectedFrom=fulltext |journal=American Journal of Physics |volume=76 |issue=8 |pages=704–719 |arxiv=0708.4249 |bibcode=2008AmJPh..76..704J |doi=10.1119/1.2904468 |issn=0002-9505}}</ref> such as [[Gustav Kirchhoff]] in a paper on the [[Huygens–Fresnel principle|Huygens principle]] in optics and by [[Oliver Heaviside]] in his work on electromagnetism.<ref name=":1" />{{Reference page|pages=|page=301}} Dirac biographer Graham Farmelo surmised that Heaviside was likely a direct influence on Dirac.<ref name=":0" />{{Reference page|page=113}} In a 1963 interview, Dirac stated, "All [[Electrical engineering|electrical engineers]] are familiar with the idea of a pulse, and the <math>\delta</math>-function is just a way of expressing a pulse mathematically."<ref name=":1" />{{Reference page|page=301}}  

''The Principles'' was atypical for its time in many different ways. It did not contain any references to the research literature. Chapter One is a purely qualitative exposition on the principle of superposition, illustrated by the [[Polarization (waves)|polarization of light]]. The [[Planck constant]] <math>h</math> was only mentioned later in the book, in a discussion on the general [[Canonical commutation relation|commutation relations]], where Dirac introduced the reduced Planck constant <math>\hslash</math> ("<math>h</math> bar" or "Dirac's <math>h</math>") as a shorthand for <math>h/2\pi</math>. Likewise, the [[Schrödinger equation]] was presented late in the book. For Dirac, quantum mechanics was no more than a mathematical framework from which one could calculate quantities that could be [[Falsifiability|compared with experiment]]. Questions of deeper meaning were, according to him, meaningless. Although Dirac never discussed the philosophy of quantum mechanics, his views were, in effect, close to the Copenhagen interpretation.<ref name=":4" /> (Also see [[positivism]].) 

In the second edition (1935), Dirac aimed to make the book more accessible than the first,<ref name=":0" />{{Reference page|pages=254-5}} and rewrote most of it.<ref name=":1" />{{Reference page|page=367}} Unlike the first edition, where he defined the "state" of a quantum-mechanical system as its condition in four-dimensional spacetime, in this edition, he only described the "state" of a system only for a given moment in time. Being aware of the difficulties of making quantum mechanics fully consistent with special relativity in order to create a coherent quantum theory of electrodynamics, he resorted to using three-dimensional space in the sense of classical physics.<ref name=":4" /> He included a new discussion on the [[Action (physics)|action principle]], though with a footnote saying that students uninterested in [[analytical mechanics]] could skip it, and acknowledged the discovery of the [[positron]], predicted by the negative-energy solution to his relativistic wave equation for the electron.<ref name=":3" /> In the first edition, Dirac, as he did in the 1928 paper, stated—erroneously—the negative-energy solution was the proton.<ref name=":4" /> Interpreting negative-energy solutions was a matter of controversy.<ref name=":03">{{cite book |last=Pais |first=Abraham |author-link=Abraham Pais |title='Subtle is the Lord..': The Science and the Life of Albert Einstein |title-link=Subtle is the Lord |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=1982 |isbn=0-19-853907-X |location=Oxford |pages=}}</ref>{{Reference page|pages=360-1}} But Hermann Weyl, J. Robert Oppenheimer, and Wolfgang Pauli showed that a "[[Dirac hole theory|hole]]" in the "[[Dirac sea|sea]]" of negative energy had the same mass as an electron. By 1931, Dirac was convinced that his equation predicted the existence of [[antimatter]].<ref name=":0" />{{Reference page|page=187}} The positron—short for "positive electron"—was discovered the following year by [[Carl David Anderson|Carl Anderson]].<ref name=":0" />{{Reference page|page=224}} 

In 1947 the third edition of the book was published, in which the chapter on quantum electrodynamics was rewritten particularly with the inclusion of [[Pair production|electron-positron creation]].<ref name="Paul Dirac" /> Beginning with this edition, the mathematical descriptions of quantum states and operators were changed to use the [[bra–ket notation]],<ref name=":3" /> introduced in 1939 by Dirac himself.<ref name="Dirac">{{cite journal |last1=Dirac |first1=P. A. M. |year=1939 |title=A new notation for quantum mechanics |journal=[[Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society]] |volume=35 |issue=3 |pages=416–418 |bibcode=1939PCPS...35..416D |doi=10.1017/S0305004100021162 |s2cid=121466183 |authorlink1=Paul Dirac}}
</ref>

In the fourth edition, 1958, the same chapter was revised, adding new sections on interpretation and applications.<ref name="Paul Dirac" /> It was later reprinted multiple times.<ref name=":4" /> A revised fourth edition appeared in 1967.<ref name="Paul Dirac" /> For the last editions, the greatest changes were in the final chapter of the book, a reflection of the rapid pace of development of quantum electrodynamics, both theoretical and experimental.<ref name=":3" /> Although Dirac knew about [[group theory]], he did not think of it as a useful tool for quantum mechanics, and consequently did not include it in his book.<ref name=":4" /> (Group theory was first applied to quantum mechanics—controversially—by [[Eugene Wigner]] and John von Neumann and independently by Hermann Weyl in the late 1920s.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Wightman |first=A.S. |author-link=Arthur Wightman |year=1995 |title=Eugene Paul Wigner 1902–1995 |url=https://www.ams.org/notices/199507/wigner.pdf |journal=[[Notices of the American Mathematical Society]] |volume=42 |issue=7 |pages=769–771}}</ref>)

== Translations ==
It has been translated to multiple languages,<ref name=":3" /> including Russian,<ref name=":3" /> Japanese,<ref name=":3" /> German,<ref name=":4" /> and French.<ref name=":1" />{{Reference page|page=300}} Dirac supplied an additional preface for the Russian edition, thanks to his good relationship with Russian physicists [[Igor Tamm]] and Peter Kapitza.<ref name=":3" /> At the request of [[Dmitri Ivanenko]], Dirac added a chapter on methods of approximations, including the [[Hartree–Fock method]] (developed by [[Douglas Hartree]] and [[Vladimir Fock]]) for the Russian edition. In the Russian edition, Ivanenko added multiple appendices and [[Matvei Bronstein]] some footnotes.<ref name=":4" /> He also supplied a preface to the Japanese edition as requested by the translators, two of whom were [[Yoshio Nishina]] and [[Sin-Itiro Tomonaga]].<ref name=":3" /> Being fluent in German, Dirac personally checked the German translation by [[Werner Bloch]].<ref name=":4" /> 

== Contents ==
* The [[Quantum superposition|principle of superposition]]
* Dynamical variables and [[Observable|observables]]
* Representations
* The [[quantum conditions]]
* The equations of motion
* Elementary applications
* [[Perturbation theory]]
* [[Scattering|Collision problems]]
* Systems containing several [[Indistinguishable particles|similar particles]]
* [[Theory of radiation]]
* [[Dirac equation|Relativistic theory of the electron]]
* [[Quantum electrodynamics]]

== Reception and legacy ==
According to [[Laurie Brown (physicist)|Laurie M. Brown]], it "set the stage, the tone, and much of the language of the quantum-mechanical revolution."<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last=Brown |first=Laurie M. |author-link=Laurie Brown (physicist) |date=2006 |title=Paul A. M. Dirac's Principles of Quantum Mechanics |url=https://faculty.washington.edu/seattle/physics441/online/about%20Dirac.pdf |journal=Physics in Perspective |volume=8 |issue=4 |pages=381–407 |bibcode=2006PhP.....8..381B |doi=10.1007/s00016-006-0276-4 |s2cid=120303937}}</ref> 

The book quickly rose to prominence, surpassing other texts published in the 1930s. German and Russian translations were even more popular. In what was then the Soviet Union, it sold 3,000 copies in just a few months. However, the publishing house, GTTI, felt the need to assert that despite appearances to the contrary, Dirac's personal view of quantum mechanics, which was close to what would later be named the [[Copenhagen interpretation]], was not at odds with the ideology of [[dialectical materialism]].<ref name=":4">{{citation |author=Helge Kragh |title=Paul Dirac and The Principles of Quantum Mechanics |year=2013 |url=https://www.mprl-series.mpg.de/studies/2/11/ |series=Research and Pedagogy, Studies 2: A History of Quantum Physics through Its Textbooks |publisher=Max-Planck-Gesellschaft zur Förderung der Wissenschaften |isbn=9783945561249}}</ref> [[Felix Bloch]] praised the book for its originality and self-contained presentation, but worried that Dirac did not refer much to the original research literature.<ref name=":4" /> Matvei Bronstein opined that Dirac's textbook was superior to ''[[Gruppentheorie und Quantenmechanik]]'' (1928) by [[Hermann Weyl]], which, according to him, was overly formal.<ref name=":4" /> [[Wolfgang Pauli]] praised it as "an indispensable standard work" but was concerned that it was too distant from experiments.<ref name=":0" />{{Reference page|page=179}} He also had a high opinion of the German translation, describing it and the original book as "highly reliable" and "essential" for physicists studying quantum theory.<ref name=":3" /> [[J. Robert Oppenheimer]] called the book an "astonishingly complete" and "coherent" treatise, comparing it to ''[[Elementary Principles in Statistical Mechanics]]'' (1902) by [[Josiah Willard Gibbs]], but warned that like Gibbs' book, it was not suitable as an introduction to quantum mechanics.<ref name=":4" /> Similarly, [[John Lennard-Jones]] recommended the book for everyone who wished to stay abreast with modern physics, but cautioned that it was not easy to read.<ref name=":4" /> [[Charles Galton Darwin]] complained about the lack of concrete examples to illustrate the theory.<ref name=":4" /> [[Paul Epstein]] and [[Werner Heisenberg]] complimented the second edition for being more comprehensible than the first.<ref name=":3" /> [[Albert Einstein]] admired the book as "the most logically perfect presentation" of the subject and made it his companion.<ref name=":0" />{{Reference page|page=179}} [[Freeman Dyson]] compared it to a fine work of art.<ref name=":0" />{{Reference page|page=428}} Indeed, while textbooks are seldom cited in research papers, Dirac's ''Principles'' proved to be an exception during the 1930s.<ref name=":4" />

However, while physicists had a high opinion of the book, mathematicians were more critical. [[Bernard Koopman]] praised Dirac for his profound physical insight but disliked what he perceived as its lack of logical clarity. Koopman also took issue with Dirac's use of the hybrid terms ''[[Eigenvalues and eigenvectors|eigenvalue]]'' and ''[[eigenfunction]]''—from the German ''Eigenwert'' and ''Eigenfunktion—''instead of ''characteristic value'' and ''characteristic function''.<ref name=":4" /> [[Garrett Birkhoff]] and [[John von Neumann]] complained about the way Dirac employed mathematics, including the <math>\delta</math>-distribution.<ref name=":4" /> [[Max Jammer]] observed that Dirac's primary motivation in writing the book was creating an exposition in physics, treating [[Applied mathematics|mathematics as a tool]]. In this regard, von Neumann's ''Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics'' (1932), with its uncompromising emphasis on [[Rigour#Mathematics|mathematical rigour]], was a supplement to Dirac's book.<ref name=":1" />{{Reference page|page=367}} Indeed, Dirac himself admitted that it was not a function in the standard sense of the term, but justified his position by arguing that his use of it nevertheless led to correct results.<ref name=":0" />{{Reference page|page=113}} On the other hand, the <math>\delta</math>-distribution was a motivation for [[Laurent Schwartz]] in his work to put the notion of [[Distribution (mathematical analysis)|distributions]] or generalized functions on a secure mathematical footing in 1945.<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal |last=Lützen|first=Jesper|author-link=Jesper Lützen|date=June 1979|title=Heaviside's Operational Calculus and the Attempts to Rigorise It|url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF00330405|journal=[[Archive for History of Exact Sciences]]|volume=21|pages=161–200|doi=10.1007/BF00330405|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Schwartz credited Dirac with thinking of the <math>\delta</math>-function as the kernel of an [[integral transform]].<ref name=":3" /> Dirac's distribution remains in use.<ref name=":5" />

Among students, opinions were mixed. Some were displeased that the book was basically a transcript of Dirac's lectures at Cambridge.<ref name=":0" />{{Reference page|page=179}} Most students looked elsewhere because they wanted a text that could teach them how to carry out computations. But the most gifted of them viewed the book as a "bible" of modern physics.<ref name=":0" />{{Reference page|page=255}} One such student was [[Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar]], who later became an astrophysicist.<ref name=":0" />{{Reference page|page=179}} [[Abdus Salam]] and [[Eugene Wigner]] compared Dirac's ''The Principles of Quantum Mechanics'' with the ''[[Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica|Principia]]'', written by Dirac's predecessor as the [[Lucasian Professor of Mathematics]] at Cambridge, [[Isaac Newton]].<ref name=":3" /> For young American physicists of the 1930s, Dirac's text was one of their first introductions to the nascent scientific theory.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Cassidy |first=David |author-link=David C. Cassidy |title=A Short History of Physics in the American Century |publisher=Harvard University Press |year=2011 |isbn=978-0-674-04936-9 |location=Cambridge, MA}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=38}} In his doctoral dissertation, [[Richard Feynman]] cited Dirac's discussion of the action principle in the second edition.<ref name=":3" /> Still in print in the early twenty-first century, it has influenced many generations of young physicists.<ref name=":0" />{{Reference page|page=428}} [[John Gribbin]] recommended that  students at least borrow a library copy to read the first chapter.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last=Gribbin |first=John |title=In Search of Schrodinger's Cat: Quantum Physics and Reality |title-link=In Search of Schrödinger's Cat |publisher=Black Swan |year=1984 |isbn=978-0-552-12555-0 |location=London}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=361}} However, Dirac biographer [[Graham Farmelo]] recalled his colleagues' complaints that the book was not useful for learning physics developed after 1940 due to Dirac's refusal to accept [[renormalization]]—which he described as something that merely "swept infinities under the carpet"—even though it had become a standard tool in [[quantum field theory]].<ref name="Farmelo" />
